newsitem.title: SURINAM: Ex-military leader wins Surinam presidential vote.
newsitem.headline: Ex-military leader wins Surinam presidential vote.

text.p: A leading member of Surinam's former military government was elected president on Thursday in the closest presidential vote since independence from the Netherlands in 1975.

Jules Wijdenbosch, 55, who is backed by former military strongman Desi Bouterse, defeated current President Ronald Venetiaan by 438 votes to 407, in a secret ballot of Surinam's top regional and national politicians.
"With this result, Jules Wijdenbosch is the new president of the country," National Assembly Speaker Jaggernath Lachmon said after the votes had been counted.
Wijdenbosch's supporters in the national sports centre where the vote took place burst into applause and sang the national anthem after learning the result.
The new president is expected to be sworn in on Sept. 14 for a five-year term.

The tense vote ended months of political uncertainty following unclear general election results in May. Neither Venetiaan's New Front coalition nor Wijdenbosch's National Democratic Party (NDP) secured the two-thirds majority necessary to form a government in the May elections.
This result forced Thursday's vote of the United Peoples Assembly (VVV) which includes over 800 national, regional and district politicians.
Wijdenbosch's victory reversed a heavy defeat in 1991 when Venetiaan became Surinam's first democratically-elected leader in over a decade.

Venetiaan, 60, had appeared to be in the driving seat after scoring a narrow victory over the NDP in May's elections. But a series of defections left the once-strong New Front coalition in tatters going into Thursday's vote.

Parties which shifted allegiance to the NDP did so on condition that former strongman Bouterse would not hold public office. Many hold him responsible for ordering the 1982 torture and murder of 15 opposition leaders.
His stern regime provoked a six-year armed uprising starting in 1986 which cost more than 500 lives and prompted about 15,000 to seek exile in neighbouring French Guiana.
Many still fear that despite Bouterse's assurances victory for Wijdenbosch will effectively place the former military strongman in power.
Bouterse named Wijdenbosch his vice president and finance minister in 1990.
